gaps.sentence: He ___ a fortune selling software online.
gaps.explanation: make a fortune means to earn a very large amount of money.

gaps.sentence: The ___ traffic added an hour to our journey.
gaps.explanation: heavy traffic means a lot of vehicles on the road; 'thick traffic' is not standard.

gaps.sentence: Our guide was highly ___ and had climbed the mountain five times.
gaps.explanation: highly experienced is the standard collocation; 'highly' combines with participial adjectives.

gaps.sentence: Grandad's best man ___ a joke that made everyone laugh.
gaps.explanation: tell a joke is the fixed collocation; 'say a joke' is not used.

gaps.sentence: The neighbours ___ a loud argument in the garden last night.
gaps.explanation: have an argument (with somebody) is the fixed collocation for quarrelling.

gaps.sentence: The roads were almost empty — the traffic was surprisingly ___.
gaps.explanation: light traffic means few vehicles on the road; its opposite is heavy traffic.

gaps.sentence: The poster in the shop window ___ my eye.
gaps.explanation: catch somebody's eye means to attract someone's attention.

gaps.sentence: I was nearly late, but I managed to ___ the last bus.
gaps.hint: to get on a bus or train in time
gaps.explanation: catch a bus/train means to arrive in time to board it; the words 'managed to' and 'nearly late' show success.
